title: Multi-agent systems: which pattern fits which task
act: Act III — Multi-agent, done on evidence
takeaway: Match the pattern to the task, compare a strong baseline, and verify the integrated result.

scenes.title: Separate the mechanisms
scenes.visual: 7.1.1: diagram lays out six mechanisms with identical request cards. 7.1.2: highlight layered proposal and synthesis, with gradeBadge A. 7.1.3–7.1.5: animate separate evidence paths, discussion edges, and router/cascade gates; do not imply equal cost. 7.1.6: highlight task fit: bounded exploration, independent search, and a sequential chain that remains intact.

sentences.text: Multi-agent design starts with the task, not with a desired headcount.
Mixture-of-Agents names a specific layered proposal-and-synthesis method published at ICLR in 2025, not every system with subagents.
sentences.spoken: Mixture of Agents names a specific layered proposal and synthesis method published at ICLR in twenty twenty five, not every system with subagents.

sentences.text: A single loop retains control; an isolated worker separates context; parallel map-and-reduce separates independent work.
Debate revises answers through discussion, while layered synthesis aggregates proposals.
Routing selects a model; a cascade can escalate until its stopping criterion is met.
Use isolated workers to contain exploration history, parallel branches for separable research, and avoid splitting a tightly dependent reasoning chain just to add participants.

onScreen.text: Six mechanisms: single loop · isolated worker · parallel map/reduce · debate · layered MoA · router/cascade
MoA: ICLR 2025 · proposal → synthesis · prompt-based answer generation, not necessarily autonomous tool use

scenes.title: What extra inference buys
scenes.visual: 7.2.1–7.2.2: pairedBars shows only the MoA comparison, with full conditions and gradeBadge A. 7.2.3: diagram swaps to independent samples and voting. 7.2.4: separate discussion panel adds the strong-prompt baseline; never combine these studies into a leaderboard.

sentences.text: The original MoA study reported 65.1 percent against GPT-4 Omni’s 57.5 percent on AlpacaEval 2.0’s length-controlled win rate.
sentences.spoken: The original MoA study reported sixty five point one percent against GPT four Omni’s fifty seven point five percent on AlpacaEval two point zero’s length controlled win rate.

sentences.text: That historical, judge-based instruction-following result is not a repository-repair success rate.
Peer-reviewed sampling-and-voting work supports trying independent candidates before adding elaborate communication.
Peer-reviewed debate results show gains, but another study found strong single-model prompting could nearly match the best discussions.

onScreen.text: MoA 65.1% ± 0.6 SD vs GPT-4 Omni (05/13) 57.5% · AlpacaEval 2.0 LC win rate · 805 instructions · 3 runs · ICLR 2025 · six proposers: Qwen1.5-110B/72B-Chat, WizardLM-8x22B, Llama-3-70B-Instruct, Mixtral-8x22B, DBRX; three layers; Qwen1.5-110B final aggregator · GPT-4-based judge/reference · not coding accuracy or a same-cost repository comparison
Sampling/voting ≠ autonomous collaboration · Debate must beat strong prompting

scenes.title: Diversity is not enough
scenes.visual: 7.3.1: diagram repeats the strongest proposer while retaining a distinct aggregator; gradeBadge A. 7.3.2: role-by-domain matrix with gradeBadge B replaces brand-colored nodes. 7.3.3: keep competence caption visible.

sentences.text: Self-MoA found repeated sampling from its strongest proposer could beat mixed proposers, while keeping a different model as aggregator.
The X-MAS preprint instead found benefits from choosing models for particular functions and domains.
The practical lesson is to preserve competence while testing useful diversity: a collection of brands is not, by itself, an architecture.

onScreen.text: Self-MoA: repeated strongest proposer; distinct aggregator retained · TMLR 2026; numerical experiment from identified preprint version
X-MAS v1 (2025-05-22): role/domain selection · not evidence that brand diversity always helps

scenes.title: Scale with care
scenes.visual: 7.4.1: statCard displays Anthropic internal result. 7.4.2: denominator diagram anchors token multiplier to chat. 7.4.3: help/hurt smallMultiples shows direction only, with v3 caveat. 7.4.4: MAST failure categories. 7.4.5: timeline explicitly advances Cognition from its earlier warning to the follow-up.

sentences.text: Anthropic reported a 90.2 percent improvement on its internal research evaluation: an Opus 4 lead with Sonnet 4 workers, compared with Opus 4 alone.
sentences.spoken: Anthropic reported a ninety point two percent improvement on its internal research evaluation: an Opus four lead with Sonnet four workers, compared with Opus four alone.

sentences.text: Its roughly fifteenfold token observation compares multi-agent systems with chat, not with a single agent.
The Science of Scaling preprint, version three, suggests benefits for parallelizable tasks and harm for sequential planning, with small coding samples.
MAST documents failures in system design, inter-agent alignment, and verification.
Cognition’s 2026 follow-up supports clean-context reviewers around a single writer, revising its earlier warning.
sentences.spoken: Cognition’s twenty twenty six follow-up supports clean-context reviewers around a single writer, revising its earlier warning.

scenes.title: Approval is not proof
scenes.visual: 7.5.1: quoteCard contrasts approval with evidence. 7.5.2: diagram gives evaluator access to files and requirements; gradeBadge A. No fabricated defect-detection score.

sentences.text: Peer-reviewed work finds self-preference in evaluation and surface-form biases in code judging, so reviewer approval cannot establish correctness.
Agent-as-a-Judge supports giving evaluators access to actual artifacts and requirements; agreement with humans still is not production bug-detection performance.

onScreen.text: Reviewed ≠ verified · inspect implementation and requirements · run external checks · judge agreement is not code pass rate

scenes.title: A conditional coding split
scenes.visual: 7.6.1–7.6.2: diagram highlights planner, navigator, editor, executor as the actual HyperAgent roles. 7.6.3: add an evidence-seeking reviewer in a dashed synthesis boundary, never attribute it as a HyperAgent role.

sentences.text: HyperAgent’s preprint supplies an early measured example of strong planning and editing with cheaper navigation and execution.
That supports a role-specific option, not a permanent model shopping list or fixed team size.
For review, ask a separate evaluator to inspect the implementation and requirements, rather than simply approve the editor’s account.

onScreen.text: HyperAgent v3 · 2025-09-05 · Planner / Navigator / Editor / Executor · historical role/model ablations; no universal recipe
Editorial synthesis — workflow option: strong planner · cheaper scouts · capable editor · evidence-seeking reviewer

scenes.title: Eleven conditional principles
scenes.visual: 7.7.1: diagram reveals all eleven principles in readable groups, with persistent High/Medium/Low text badges distinct from evidence grades. 7.7.2: emphasize low direct evidence for cross-family defect detection. 7.7.3: highlight separate latency and total-compute meters. 7.7.4: settle all eleven into the checklist for the closing sentence and final hold.

sentences.text: The research points to eleven conditional principles, with confidence levels that distinguish well-supported recommendations from experiments still worth testing.
Cross-family review has low direct evidence for superior defect detection; treat it as an experiment.
Track latency and total compute separately: parallel completion can be faster while consuming more resources overall.
Start simple, delegate separable work through explicit contracts, preserve evidence, and verify whether the coordination actually pays.

onScreen.text: 11 principles · our conditional synthesis of the evidence · confidence is not source grade
1. Start with a strong simple baseline — High confidence
2. Parallelize separable information or independent candidates — High confidence
3. Keep one integration owner for coupled edits; explicit ownership/dependencies for multi-writer teams — Medium confidence
4. Define tasks as contracts, not job titles — High confidence
5. Choose models by measured role performance — High confidence
6. Cheap scouts plus strong planner: an option, not a shopping list — Medium confidence
7. Preserve consequential decisions and provenance in handoffs — High confidence
8. Seek evidence and external checks; reviewed is not verified — High confidence
9. Try cross-family review as an ablation, not an assurance — Low for superior defect detection; medium as a bias-mitigation hypothesis
10. Control budget, latency, and communication separately — High confidence
11. Re-evaluate after changing model or harness — High confidence
